newsitem.title: UK: UK stocks outlook- Focus on earnings and U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: UK stocks outlook- Focus on earnings and U.S. data.

text.p: UK stocks took a breather from the market's recent violent swings on Friday as investors braced themselves for an onslaught of major company results and July's key U.S. employment report next week.
"Things really take off next week with the interim reporting season and people will want to keep their powder dry until they hear what these companies have to say," said one equity salesman.

After soaring to the brink of the psychological 5,000 barrier the previous week, the leading FTSE 100 index put in a more subdued performance ahead of the slew of company results to be down around 40 points on the week at 4,839 by mid-afternoon.

"The volatility we have seen in the market shows that London is very uncertain about where it wants to go in the short term," the salesman said. "People are nervous about interest rates and sterling -- there are a lot of reasons to be cautious."
But Robert Buckland, UK equities strategist at HSBC James Capel reckons that the sheer weight of money still being held in cash will support the market on any weakness.
"At the moment I'm quite happy to see a bit of consolidation and my recommendation to clients is to buy on these dips," he said.
Among the companies reporting next week are some of Britain's biggest, including Glaxo Wellcome, BT, Lloyds TSB and Abbey National.
Sterling's seemingly relentless rise to seven-and-a-half year highs will remain in the spotlight as engineering group TI also reports on its progress.
"The main focus will be what manufacturers are telling us about the impact of sterling," Buckland said. "We know it's not good news but we want to see just how bad it is."
Unilever, Lasmo, Guardian Royal Exchange and BAT complete the line-up of FTSE companies reporting earnings.
But the event most likely to set nerves jangling will be across the Atlantic and the July U.S. non-farm payrolls figures which have in the past sent global stock markets spinning.
"Obviously, the U.S. payrolls data is the big number of the week," Buckland commented. "It's more important than any UK data for driving the markets."

In June, the report signalled only moderate growth in wages and jobs, calming worries about the potential for a near-term U.S. interest rate rise. The Dow has since continued to set record upon record on hopes that the "goldilocks" scenario of growth without inflation will continue.

Meanwhile in the UK, after three interest rate rises in as many months, the surge in consumer demand shows no sign of abating and analysts remained wary of another rate hike after the next monetary policy meeting in August.
"The pressure here is still on rates going up," Buckland said. "But for the moment, the market seems to be taking all these rate hikes on the chin."
